extracted.intended_audience: public administration and social science researchers, survey methodologists, and policymakers interested in public opinion on AI governance
extracted.subtask_short: survey measurement of AI policy preferences
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, measuring, and analyzing survey constructs about public support for AI regulation (softer and stronger policies), institutional and technology trust, perceived risk, and relevant controls in a nationally representative U.S. sample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for slowing down AI development
rubrics_metrics.description: Composite variable: the average of three items — “I support public campaigns to slow down AI development,” “I support government regulation that slows down AI development,” and “I oppose government regulation that slows down AI development” (the opposition item reverse-coded). Each item measured on 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree) Likert-type scales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use averaging after reverse-coding where necessary. This captures a 'softer' regulatory preference. Inspired by prior moratorium proposals (Metzinger, 2021). Report means, SDs, and internal consistency (Cronbach’s α).

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for banning advanced AI technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Composite variable: the average of three items — “I support banning the development of artificial general intelligence that is smarter than humans,” “I support a global ban on data centers that are large enough to train AI systems that are smarter than humans,” and “I support a global ban on the development of sentience in robots/AIs.” Items measured on 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat as measure of stronger regulatory preference (bans). Average items to form index; report reliability and descriptive statistics. Use clear wording to capture public support for prohibitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust in government (index)
rubrics_metrics.description: Index (average) of three items intended as proxies for governmental competency to manage and regulate AI: (1) extent of trust in governments (1 not at all to 7 very much sliding scale), (2) agreement that governments have power to effectively enforce regulations (1 strongly disagree to 7 strongly agree), and (3) categorical item transformed to numeric (no=1, not sure=4, yes=7) asking whether governments have power to regulate AI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principal component/factor analysis (eigenvalue reported) and Cronbach’s α should be used to assess construct validity (authors report eigenvalue=1.07 and provide robustness checks). Because some items may tap competency/power rather than pure affective trust, also run robustness checks with a single-item trust measure. Report both index and single-item results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust in AI industry (companies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Index (average) of three items measuring perceptions of AI creators: (1) extent of trust in companies (1 not at all to 7 very much sliding scale), (2) whether creators put safety over profits (categorical transformed to numeric), and (3) whether creators can control current and future versions of the AI (categorical transformed to numeric).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Average items into an industry-trust index; transform categorical responses to numeric consistently (no=1, not sure=4, yes=7). Assess reliability and consider conceptual overlap with government trust and AI-trust in correlations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust in AI technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Index (average) of four items using the stem 'I trust' paired with ‘chatbots,’ ‘large language models,’ ‘robots,’ and ‘game-playing AI,’ each measured 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this index to capture technology-specific trust distinct from institutional trust. Report Cronbach’s α and correlations with institutional trust measures to show discriminant validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived risk of AI
rubrics_metrics.description: Composite (average) of four items: 'AI is likely to cause human extinction,' 'Robots/AIs may be harmful to me personally,' 'Robots/AIs may be harmful to people in the USA,' and 'Robots/AIs may be harmful to future generations of people,' measured 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame items to capture safety-related risk perceptions; average into an index and report effect sizes. Authors note links to extreme-risk discourse and climate-risk measurement analogs. Use perceived risk as a key predictor of regulatory preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposure frequency / familiarity with AI
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure of how frequently respondents are exposed to or familiar with AI (presented in tables as 'Exposure Frequency'); used as a predictor and control (higher exposure predicted less support for slowing down).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include as a covariate to capture experience/familiarity effects. Specify coding/scaling in methods; interpret negative association with support for regulation as greater familiarity reducing support for slowdown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demographic control variables and coding conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Baseline controls include gender (male=0, female=1), age, income (per 1K dollars), race/ethnicity (reference group Asian American), political orientation (coded from very liberal=1 to very conservative=5), education, and other listed racial/ethnic categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use standard coding and explicitly report reference groups. Include demographics in baseline model to assess incremental explanatory power of theoretical predictors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Likert scales and reverse-coding practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 1–7 Likert-type scales for many items; reverse-code items where wording is oppositional (e.g., 'I oppose government regulation that slows down AI development') prior to inclusion in composites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure consistent directionality across items before averaging. Report exact scale anchors and reverse-coding steps in methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transforming categorical responses to numeric scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorical items with responses like 'no,' 'not sure,' and 'yes' were converted to numeric values (no = 1, not sure = 4, yes = 7) to align with 1–7 scales for inclusion in indices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When combining categorical and Likert items into indices, map categories to the same numeric range thoughtfully (authors chose equidistant mapping). Report transformation and justify it; check sensitivity to alternative mappings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability and construct validity checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Report Cronbach’s α for multi-item constructs (authors report α values for several indices) and perform principal component/factor analysis (report eigenvalues and explained variance) to assess unidimensionality and validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide α, factor eigenvalues, and PCA variance proportions. If α is low or factor eigenvalue small, report alternative specifications (e.g., single-item measures) as robustness checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multicollinearity diagnostics (VIF)
rubrics_metrics.description: Check Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) to assess multicollinearity; authors considered VIF values below 5 (mean VIF=1.9) to indicate multicollinearity is not a concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report VIFs for predictors and use conventional thresholds (e.g., VIF>5 or >10) to flag problems. If multicollinearity exists, consider variable selection or orthogonalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic choice: Seemingly Unrelated Regressions (SUR)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the two dependent variables (support for slowing down and support for bans) are strongly positively correlated (r = 0.64), SUR models were used to correlate residuals across equations and obtain more efficient estimates than separate OLS regressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use SUR when multiple related outcome equations have correlated errors. Test significance of residual correlation with the Breusch–Pagan test of independence; report correlation(ϵϵ′) and Breusch–Pagan X2 and p-values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling strategy: hierarchical model building
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt hierarchical approach with Model 1 (baseline demographics), Model 2 (adds trust predictors), and Model 3 (adds perceived risk). Compare variance explained (R2) across models to assess incremental contribution of predictor blocks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stepwise/hierarchical modeling to show incremental validity of theoretical constructs. Report change in R2 and interpret increases in explanatory power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect size interpretation thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors' ad hoc thresholds for standardized coefficients: < .20 = small effects, .20–.50 = moderate effects, > .50 = large effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State thresholds used for interpreting coefficient magnitudes; provide context by comparing to prior literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness checks and alternative specifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform robustness checks such as re-running SURs using a single-item government trust measure (instead of the index) and comparing effect sizes and significance; note covariance between measures that may influence results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always report robustness checks (alternative operationalizations, single-item vs index, transformed vs raw coding) and discuss how findings change or remain consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations: common source bias and remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge potential common source bias from cross-sectional surveys measuring key variables in a single instrument; the recommended remedy is to rely on independent data sources or deliberate survey design to separate measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss common-source bias as limitation and, where possible, incorporate design features (temporal separation, multiple data sources) or analytic strategies to mitigate it. Provide OSF preregistry and data-access information for transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling and generalizability reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a nationally representative U.S. sample (AIMS supplemental survey); explicitly state the sample frame, representativeness, and caution that findings may not generalize cross-nationally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report sampling design, sample size (authors report N=1098), and discuss external validity limits. Encourage replication in other countries and repeated measures over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regression reporting conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Report standardized beta coefficients with t-statistics in parentheses, significance stars (* p<0.05, ** p<0.01, *** p<0.001), model information such as N and R2, and postestimation statistics (e.g., correlation of residuals, Breusch–Pagan test).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow clear table conventions for ease of interpretation. Provide both standardized and unstandardized coefficients where useful, and include diagnostics for model fit and assumptions.
